paragraphs: Researchers often compare artificial and biological neural systems by fitting a regression from a network’s responses to measured brain responses. Several networks can achieve similarly good predictions, leaving a basic interpretive problem: equal prediction accuracy does not explain whether the networks represent information in similar ways.

This paper applies a theoretical framework connecting regression generalization error to spectral properties of the model and prediction target. It separates neural prediction error into contributions from the model’s eigenspectrum, the alignment between model eigenvectors and neural responses, and the amount of training data. The authors then introduce geometric measures that make these contributions easier to interpret.

Tests across many deep networks predicting visual cortical activity show that different representational geometries can produce low regression error. Consequently, a strong prediction score can arise through multiple geometric arrangements. The contribution is a more informative way to examine what that score reflects, helping researchers distinguish how different models capture neural activity even when their overall predictive performance looks similar.
neurips-2023-a-spectral-theory-of-neural.tldr: A spectral decomposition explains how different neural-network representations can achieve similarly accurate predictions of brain activity.

paragraphs: The vulnerability of classifiers to adversarial examples has inspired theoretical arguments that such failures might be unavoidable. This paper questions how directly those arguments apply to natural data. Its starting point is that broad statements about possible input distributions may miss the structure that makes robust recognition possible for particular distributions.

The authors theoretically identify concentration on small-volume regions of the input space as a key property determining whether a robust classifier exists. This shifts attention toward where the data actually lie. The relevant question becomes how the geometry of that distribution affects the possibility of robustness, rather than treating every distribution as interchangeable.

They also examine distributions concentrated on a union of low-dimensional linear subspaces. In that setting, using the data’s structure yields classifiers with data-dependent polyhedral robustness guarantees: certified regions whose geometry reflects the distribution. These guarantees improve on existing certification methods in certain regimes. The result therefore supports a conditional route to robustness based on distributional structure, while preserving the distinction between robust classifiers being possible and a universal solution for all data.
neurips-2023-adversarial-examples-might-.tldr: The paper shows how data concentration can determine whether robust classifiers exist and enable stronger certification in certain structured settings.

paragraphs: Shortening a privacy policy does not necessarily make it understandable. Extracting important sentences can preserve the same technical and legal language that confused readers in the original document. This paper addresses that readability problem for Chinese application privacy policies through both expert-annotated data and a system that rewrites relevant passages.

CAPP-130 contains 130 policies from popular applications, with 52,489 annotations and 20,555 rewritten sentences prepared through legal-expert annotation and interpretation. The accompanying framework first identifies sentences connected to a topic chosen by the user. A generative model then rewrites those sentences into a more comprehensible summary, separating topic selection from language simplification.

For the implemented summarization tool, the authors select RoBERTa for extraction after comparing six classification models and mT5 for rewriting after comparing five generative models. Their experiments report better Chinese privacy-policy summarization than GPT-4 and other baselines, including strong readability and reliability. The contribution connects the data needed to learn understandable explanations with a practical pipeline that addresses what a user wants to understand.
neurips-2023-capp-130-a-corpus-of-chines.tldr: CAPP-130 pairs expert-interpreted Chinese privacy policies with a system that extracts user-relevant passages and rewrites them into understandable summaries.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships from observational time series becomes harder when the mechanisms generating the observations change over time. This paper studies a particular form of that change: a finite collection of causal mechanisms appears in a recurring, periodic sequence. The authors call these semi-stationary time series, a setting that can represent patterns such as seasonality and daily variation.

Their algorithm, PCMCIΩ, tracks these alternating and recurring mechanisms before identifying the underlying causal graph. It uses conditional independence tests, which ask whether relationships between variables remain after accounting for other variables. The method is constraint-based and non-parametric, providing a way to search for causal structure within the specified recurring-mechanism setting.

The authors establish soundness for identifying causal relationships in discrete time series. They also evaluate the algorithm using simulated continuous and discrete data and apply it to a climate dataset. The theoretical guarantee and the experiments have different scopes: the proof concerns discrete series, while the evaluations explore a broader range of data. The central advance is accommodating structured recurring change within causal discovery.
neurips-2023-causal-discovery-in-semi-st.tldr: PCMCIΩ discovers causal structure in time series whose mechanisms recur periodically, with a soundness guarantee for discrete series.

paragraphs: Irregular time series require a model to account for observations arriving at uneven intervals while representing changes that happen continuously. The paper describes a tension between existing approaches: discrete neural architectures can model complex relationships, while Neural ODE approaches represent continuous dynamics but often struggle with intricate correlations among observations.

ContiFormer combines these abilities by extending Transformer relation modeling into continuous time. Its design brings together the attention mechanism used to represent relationships between observations and the continuous-dynamics modeling of Neural ODEs. The purpose is to describe both how a system evolves over time and how its observed data points relate to one another.

The authors mathematically characterize the model’s expressive power. With suitable choices of function hypotheses, many Transformer variants designed for irregular time series become special cases of ContiFormer. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior modeling and prediction performance. Together, these results present ContiFormer as both a unifying formulation for several existing designs and an effective approach in the evaluated irregular-time-series settings.
neurips-2023-contiformer-continuous-time.tldr: ContiFormer combines continuous-time dynamics with Transformer attention to model relationships and make predictions from irregular time series.

paragraphs: Code completion in a real repository often depends on definitions and relationships spread across multiple files. Benchmarks focused on a single file can miss this requirement. CrossCodeEval evaluates whether a model can use information elsewhere in a repository to complete code accurately, making cross-file understanding central to the task.

The benchmark draws from real, permissively licensed repositories in Python, Java, TypeScript, and C#. The authors use static analysis to locate dependencies on other files and construct examples that require that context. This construction matters because it makes access to repository information part of what the evaluation tests, rather than an optional source of extra clues.

Experiments with models including CodeGen and StarCoder find the benchmark especially difficult when relevant cross-file context is missing. Adding that context to the prompt clearly improves results, yet substantial room for improvement remains even for the strongest evaluated model. The authors also compare retrieval methods, allowing the benchmark to assess both finding useful repository context and using it to generate a completion.
neurips-2023-crosscodeeval-a-diverse-and.tldr: CrossCodeEval tests code completion that requires information from other files, exposing challenges in both retrieving and using repository context.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time-varying variables together requires understanding both patterns over time and relationships between variables. The authors’ analysis of real-world data identifies two difficulties that existing methods handle poorly: temporal fluctuations and differences among variables. CrossGNN addresses both by refining which interactions its graph neural networks emphasize.

An adaptive multi-scale identifier first constructs versions of the time series at multiple scales with reduced noise. A cross-scale graph network then extracts scales showing clearer trends and weaker noise. A separate cross-variable graph network models both similarities and differences among variables, allowing the forecasting system to use these distinct kinds of relationships together.

The model emphasizes edges with higher saliency scores while constraining lower-scoring edges. This design allows time and space complexity to scale linearly with input sequence length. Experiments on eight real-world multivariate time-series datasets demonstrate effectiveness compared with state-of-the-art methods. The approach connects noise handling and interaction selection: its forecasting representation depends on choosing informative temporal scales and variable relationships while controlling the cost of processing longer sequences.
neurips-2023-crossgnn-confronting-noisy-.tldr: CrossGNN refines interactions across time scales and variables to forecast noisy multivariate series with linear complexity in sequence length.

paragraphs: Many learning problems involve dividing elements into mutually exclusive groups without knowing the number of groups beforehand. The elements might be data samples or neurons in a network layer. Because group assignments and the number of groups are discrete, directly learning such partitions creates an obstacle for end-to-end gradient-based optimization.

This paper introduces a random partition model that separates the decision into two stages. It first infers how many elements belong in each subset, then fills those subsets according to a learned ordering. The construction enables reparameterized gradients with respect to the partition model’s parameters, allowing partition inference to participate in variational inference tasks.

The authors demonstrate the approach in three settings: variational clustering, learning shared and independent generative factors with weak supervision, and multitask learning. These applications illustrate the breadth of a common underlying operation: learning how elements should be grouped as part of a larger model. The contribution is a general-purpose way to make that operation compatible with gradient-based learning, supported by demonstrations across distinct tasks.
neurips-2023-differentiable-random-parti.tldr: A two-stage random partition model enables gradient-based learning of groupings with an unknown number of subsets.

paragraphs: Understanding conversation involves more than recognizing the literal meaning of individual sentences. A listener must interpret what a speaker means in a particular situation, using context and knowledge to resolve ambiguity or figurative language. DiPlomat turns this pragmatic reasoning problem into a benchmark for conversational language models.

The authors collect a human-annotated dataset containing 4,177 multi-turn dialogues and a vocabulary of 48,900 words. The benchmark covers reasoning about situational context, acquiring open-world knowledge, and understanding figurative language. It introduces two evaluation tasks: Pragmatic Reasoning and Identification, and Conversational Question Answering. These provide ways to examine interpretation within conversations rather than treating utterances as isolated text.

The paper also investigates a zero-shot natural language inference task, emphasizing the importance of context for pragmatic reasoning. Experiments reveal limitations in the evaluated leading language models’ handling of these conversational demands. The dataset and tasks provide concrete evaluation targets for improving nuanced language understanding, while the findings motivate further work toward conversational agents that better recognize socially and emotionally meaningful intent.
neurips-2023-diplomat-a-dialogue-dataset.tldr: DiPlomat evaluates whether language models can interpret conversational meaning using context, outside knowledge, and figurative-language understanding.

paragraphs: Brain-age prediction uses imaging data to estimate an individual’s apparent brain age. A difference between that estimate and chronological age can reflect accelerated aging and increased vulnerability to neurological disease or cognitive impairment. The paper addresses an interpretability problem: a single age-gap value provides little anatomical explanation for the model’s estimate.

The authors build a framework using coVariance neural networks and cortical thickness features. Their aim is to connect predictions to identifiable brain regions. In the Alzheimer’s disease setting they study, the networks can identify anatomical regions contributing to an elevated predicted brain-age gap, adding an explanation to the overall age estimate.

A second observation links that interpretability to the model’s use of specific eigenvectors of the anatomical covariance matrix. These eigenvectors describe particular patterns within the covariance structure, and exploiting them is a condition for the reported interpretability. The contribution therefore connects a regional explanation of brain-age predictions with a mathematical property of the network’s representation, extending the analysis beyond the coarse age-gap measurement.
neurips-2023-explainable-brain-age-predi.tldr: CoVariance neural networks connect elevated brain-age predictions in Alzheimer’s disease to contributing brain regions through specific covariance patterns.

paragraphs: Analyses of message-passing graph neural networks often ask whether they can distinguish two graphs, using the one-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman test as a reference. That binary question leaves out degrees of similarity. This paper develops a continuous perspective that also describes how difficult graphs are to separate.

The authors extend both the test and message-passing networks to graphons, continuous representations used in graph theory. They characterize the networks’ expressive power through a topology describing distinguishability and closeness, and prove a universal approximation theorem. They also connect this characterization to tree distance, based on fractional isomorphisms, and counts expressed through tree homomorphisms. These different descriptions have equivalent expressive power in the studied setting.

Experiments show that randomly initialized networks can perform competitively with trained counterparts in the evaluations. The authors also compare architectures by their ability to preserve graph distances. The combined contribution is a framework for interpreting graph representations through similarity and geometry, alongside distinguishability, with empirical evidence that these theoretical relationships illuminate network behavior.
neurips-2023-fine-grained-expressivity-o.tldr: A continuous extension of the Weisfeiler–Leman test characterizes both graph distinguishability and similarity for message-passing neural networks.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement-learning agents can receive several kinds of input, such as color images, depth, and event data. A common approach fuses their features and uses one critic to estimate value from the combined representation. The paper argues that this can overlook the distinct contribution each modality makes to learning a policy.

HAVE introduces local, modality-specific value estimation. It dynamically estimates the contribution of each modality and adjusts its importance at the value level. A further task-contextual fusion process rebalances information from both features and value estimates. This hierarchy coordinates the usefulness of individual inputs with what they contribute collectively.

The authors report substantially improved agent performance and examine autonomous driving using the CARLA benchmark with event and depth data. Their evaluations also demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework’s distinct components. The approach matters because combining sensors involves more than placing their features together: estimating their separate contributions gives the agent an additional way to adapt how it uses complementary information for its task.
neurips-2023-hierarchical-adaptive-value.tldr: HAVE improves multimodal reinforcement learning by adaptively balancing each modality’s value contribution alongside their combined features.

paragraphs: Training on web image–text pairs can teach a vision model through different objectives. Contrastive training learns representations by comparing paired and unpaired examples, while captioning trains a model to generate text about an image. This paper examines whether captioning has been underestimated as a way to learn useful visual representations.

The authors compare the approaches while matching training data, computation, and model capacity. Using a standard encoder–decoder Transformer, they find that captioning alone produces vision encoders competitive with contrastively trained encoders on classification tasks. On tasks involving both vision and language, the captioning-trained encoders outperform the contrastive counterparts in their evaluation.

The study also examines architecture, model scale, and pretraining data. Captioning shows equal or better scaling behavior along these dimensions. These results make the comparison relevant beyond a single training configuration: the reported effectiveness persists as key ingredients vary. The finding is that a plain caption-generation objective can provide strong visual pretraining, with the relative outcome depending on the kind of downstream task being evaluated.
neurips-2023-image-captioners-are-scalab.tldr: Under matched training conditions, image captioning learns competitive classification features and stronger vision–language features than contrastive pretraining in the evaluations.

paragraphs: Open-ended chat assistants are difficult to evaluate because conventional benchmarks do not fully capture what people prefer in a conversation. This paper investigates whether strong language models can judge other models’ responses, offering a more scalable way to approximate expensive human preference assessments.

The authors introduce MT-Bench, a set of multi-turn questions, and Chatbot Arena, a platform for crowdsourced model comparisons. They examine agreement between model judges and human judgments while also studying position bias, preferences for verbosity, self-enhancement bias, and limited reasoning ability. They propose ways to mitigate some of these problems, making the evaluation of the judge itself part of the contribution.

Strong judges such as GPT-4 achieve over 80% agreement with controlled and crowdsourced human preferences, comparable to the reported agreement between humans. Evaluations of LLaMA and Vicuna variants also show that these conversational benchmarks complement traditional benchmarks. The findings support language-model judging as a scalable, explainable approximation of human preferences, with the identified biases remaining relevant to how its judgments are interpreted.
neurips-2023-judging-llm-as-a-judge-with.tldr: MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena show that strong language-model judges can closely approximate human preferences while exhibiting identifiable evaluation biases.

paragraphs: Coupled oscillators appear in machine-learning architectures for sequence modeling, graph representations, and physical neural networks used in analog devices. This paper asks a theoretical question about that approach: how broad a class of time-dependent relationships can an oscillator-based system represent?

The authors introduce an abstract class of neural oscillators encompassing these architectures and prove a universality result. The class can approximate continuous, causal operators between time-varying functions to a desired accuracy. An operator here maps an entire time-dependent input to a time-dependent output; causality means that the output does not require future input. The theorem therefore concerns expressive capacity for this specified class of relationships.

The proof rests on a more basic sufficiency result: forced harmonic oscillators combined with a nonlinear readout can approximate the relevant operators. This identifies a relatively simple set of ingredients capable of supporting the broader universality claim. The contribution provides a mathematical justification for oscillator-based learning systems by establishing what they can represent, with continuity and causality defining the scope of the stated result.
neurips-2023-neural-oscillators-are-univ.tldr: The paper proves that neural oscillators can approximate continuous causal operators, with forced harmonic oscillators and nonlinear readouts providing sufficient ingredients.

paragraphs: Inductive conformal prediction expresses uncertainty by returning a set of possible answers with a high-probability coverage guarantee. Useful sets should also be efficient in their size and contents. Learning model and scoring parameters to improve those properties creates a challenge: gains on calibration data may fail to preserve efficiency or coverage on test data.

This paper uses PAC-Bayes theory to derive generalization bounds for both coverage and efficiency. Those bounds can be optimized to improve efficiency while satisfying a desired test-coverage requirement. The framework permits using the entire calibration dataset to learn model and score parameters, avoiding the separate holdout set required by the compared approach.

The authors turn the theory into an algorithm that jointly fine-tunes the prediction model and score function using calibration data. Evaluations on regression and classification tasks outperform baselines using a Hoeffding-bound-based PAC guarantee, especially when data are scarce. The contribution brings the optimization objective and its statistical guarantees together, making calibration data useful for learning efficient prediction sets while retaining guarantees about their test-time behavior.
neurips-2023-pac-bayes-generalization-ce.tldr: PAC-Bayes bounds enable learning more efficient conformal prediction sets from the full calibration dataset while certifying test-time coverage and efficiency.

paragraphs: Updating a language model with a fact is only part of making that knowledge useful. The model must also draw inferences that depend on the update. This paper addresses the gap between successfully inserting information about an entity and having that information influence the model’s broader responses.

The method has two stages. First, the authors prompt a language model with an entity definition and generate continuations to form a transfer set. Second, they update a student model so that its output distribution on that set matches a teacher distribution conditioned on the definition. This distills the behavior supported by the supplied definition into the model’s parameters.

Experiments find that the approach propagates updates more effectively than fine-tuning and other gradient-based knowledge-editing methods. The authors also report preserved performance in other contexts when injecting definitions for as many as 150 entities at once. The result supports using definition-conditioned behavior as a training signal for broader inference, extending the effect of an update beyond reproducing the inserted information.
neurips-2023-propagating-knowledge-updat.tldr: Context distillation helps language models use newly injected entity knowledge in broader inferences while preserving other-context performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A language model’s first answer may leave room for improvement even when the model already has useful capabilities. Self-Refine treats generation as an iterative process: produce an initial response, examine it, and revise it. The central idea is that the same model can perform all three roles.

After generating an answer, the model provides feedback on its own output and uses that feedback to produce a refinement. This cycle repeats, allowing later outputs to build on explicit criticism of earlier ones. The method operates at test time and requires neither supervised training data nor additional training or reinforcement learning.

The authors evaluate Self-Refine with GPT-3.5, ChatGPT, and GPT-4 across seven tasks, including dialogue generation and mathematical reasoning. Human assessments and automatic metrics favor the refined outputs over conventional single-step generation across all evaluated tasks, with an average absolute task-performance improvement of about 20%. The findings show that, in these evaluations, a model’s existing abilities can be used more effectively through repeated feedback and revision.
neurips-2023-self-refine-iterative-refin.tldr: Self-Refine improves language-model outputs at test time by repeatedly using the same model to generate feedback and revise its answers.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, trains a neural network by minimizing the sharpness of its training loss. Its established motivation is improved generalization. This paper investigates an additional effect: features at different network layers become lower rank, meaning their representations span fewer independent directions.

The authors observe this effect across fully connected networks, convolutional networks, and vision Transformers. It also appears across regression, classification, and language–image contrastive objectives. To explain the phenomenon, they examine a simple two-layer network and find that SAM entirely prunes a substantial number of activations, directly contributing to the reduced feature rank.

They support this mechanism theoretically and check that activation pruning can also occur in deeper networks. The paper explicitly notes that the full explanation can be more complex in architectures with pre-activation skip connections and self-attention. Its contribution is therefore both a broad observation about learned representations and a concrete mechanism explaining part of it, with the simpler analysis providing a starting point for understanding more elaborate networks.
neurips-2023-sharpness-aware-minimizatio.tldr: SAM reduces feature rank across diverse networks and objectives, with activation pruning explaining part of the effect.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits with knapsacks model repeated choices that produce rewards and incur several kinds of costs. The learner seeks high cumulative reward while keeping accumulated costs within budgets. This paper focuses on much tighter total-cost constraints than earlier approaches accommodated, motivated by equalizing average costs between groups.

The setting assumes continuously varying contexts, potentially signed costs, and unknown expected reward and cost functions that can be uniformly estimated. Earlier total-cost requirements were at least on the order of T to the three-quarter power, with budgets often assumed proportional to the number of rounds T. For the motivating fairness constraint, the desired budget instead approaches the natural fluctuation scale of the square root of T.

The authors introduce a dual strategy using projected gradient descent and carefully adapted step sizes. It handles total-cost constraints at the square-root scale, up to polylogarithmic factors, while offering a more direct and simpler strategy than existing approaches. This makes the bandit framework applicable to tighter group-cost balancing requirements under the stated estimation and cost assumptions.
neurips-2023-small-total-cost-constraint.tldr: An adaptive dual strategy handles near-square-root total-cost budgets in contextual bandits, supporting tighter equalized-average-cost constraints between groups.

paragraphs: Inverse rendering aims to recover properties of a scene or object from images, including shape, material, and lighting. Evaluating those properties requires suitable reference data. The paper identifies a gap in real-world datasets: object shapes and photographs from multiple viewpoints alone are insufficient for quantitatively assessing material recovery and relighting.

Stanford-ORB supplies real objects captured across varied natural scenes, together with reference 3D scans, multi-view images, and environment lighting. Combining these measurements supports evaluation of more aspects of inverse rendering within real environments. This addresses the dependence on synthetic evaluation, whose results do not by themselves establish generalization to complex real scenes.

The authors use the dataset to establish a comprehensive benchmark and compare existing inverse-rendering methods. The contribution is the evaluation resource and its accompanying comparisons, providing a shared basis for measuring progress across object-recovery tasks. By including lighting alongside geometry and images, the benchmark extends what researchers can quantitatively examine when assessing recovered materials and the appearance of objects under changed illumination.
neurips-2023-stanford-orb-a-real-world-3.tldr: Stanford-ORB combines real-object scans, multi-view images, and environment lighting to benchmark inverse rendering beyond shape recovery.

paragraphs: Structured prediction relies on surrogate losses that can be optimized in place of the prediction objective of interest. A central theoretical question is whether reducing the surrogate loss meaningfully improves the target objective. This paper studies that connection through H-consistency bounds, which account for the actual hypothesis set available to the learner.

Unlike asymptotic Bayes-consistency statements, these bounds provide a non-asymptotic perspective tied to the chosen model class. The authors first establish a negative result: widely used structured-prediction surrogate losses do not admit non-trivial H-consistency bounds. They then introduce structured comp-sum losses and structured constrained losses for which such bounds can be proved.

The new families also satisfy Bayes-consistency and yield structured-prediction algorithms through their minimization. The paper describes efficient optimization algorithms for several proposed losses, including a structured logistic loss. Its contribution connects the choice of training objective to stronger guarantees relevant to a learner’s hypothesis set, then provides optimization procedures that make several of those theoretically supported objectives usable.
neurips-2023-structured-prediction-with-.tldr: New structured-prediction surrogate losses provide non-asymptotic consistency bounds that account for the learner’s hypothesis class.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents may need to use long histories when their current observations reveal only part of the environment. Structured state space models offer long-sequence modeling, fast inference, and parallelizable training. This paper adapts a variant of S4 so that hidden states can be initialized and reset in parallel for reinforcement-learning tasks.

The modified architecture has better asymptotic scaling with sequence length than Transformers and outperforms recurrent neural networks on a simple memory task. Across the evaluated partially observable environments, it also performs better than recurrent networks while running more than five times faster. These findings connect its sequence-processing advantages with measured agent performance.

The authors further test a challenging meta-learning setting with randomly sampled continuous-control environments and randomly sampled linear projections of observations and actions. The model achieves strong performance and adapts to held-out tasks outside the training distribution. Together, the results support structured state space models as an effective architecture for the evaluated in-context reinforcement-learning problems, including tasks requiring memory and adaptation from extended interaction histories.
neurips-2023-structured-state-space-mode.tldr: A modified structured state space model delivers fast, effective reinforcement learning with memory and adaptation across the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Models such as CLIP support image–text applications by comparing their learned representations with a dot product. During training, however, the contrastive objective uses both positive and negative examples. This paper argues that ordinary dot-product inference retains only a zeroth-order approximation of that objective, discarding information relevant to how the representations were learned.

Distribution Normalization addresses the mismatch during inference. It approximates the mean representation of a batch of test samples and uses that mean as an analogue of negative-sample information in the InfoNCE training loss. This provides a computationally efficient way to incorporate information about the test distribution into the comparison procedure.

The method requires no retraining or fine-tuning and can be applied directly at test time. Experiments across a wide variety of downstream tasks show an advantage over ordinary dot-product comparisons, including alongside existing test-time augmentation methods. The contribution demonstrates that the inference rule itself can improve how a pretrained representation is used, by bringing it closer to the structure of the objective that shaped it.
neurips-2023-test-time-distribution-norm.tldr: Distribution Normalization uses test-batch representation statistics to improve contrastive vision–language inference without retraining.

paragraphs: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning starts from previously collected data and then fine-tunes through new interactions. Distribution shift complicates this transition, so existing methods constrain policy improvement. The paper argues that using one balance between improvement and constraint across all states can waste useful differences in the quality of available data.

FamO2O makes that balance depend on the state. A universal model learns a family of policies with different improvement and constraint intensities. A separate balance model selects an appropriate policy for each state. This allows existing algorithms to vary how strongly they pursue improvement and how tightly they remain constrained within a single framework.

The theoretical result establishes that state-adaptive balances are necessary for achieving a higher policy-performance upper bound. This concerns the bound, while the empirical evidence separately shows statistically significant improvements over several existing methods and state-of-the-art performance on D4RL. Together, the results motivate adapting the improvement–constraint tradeoff to local data quality and show that the proposed family-and-selection design works effectively in the evaluated benchmark.
neurips-2023-train-once-get-a-family-sta.tldr: FamO2O learns a family of policies and selects state-specific improvement–constraint balances, improving offline-to-online reinforcement learning in the reported evaluations.
